subject: physics_2
question_text: Describe Rutherford atom model. What are the drawbacks of this model?

mark_split.label: The electrons and the empty space

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. The book prints "draw backs" as two words in the question; it is written "drawbacks" here and the wording is unchanged. The book's own limitation list for this question repeats the electron-structure point; the card gives the two standard drawbacks instead, each with its reason. Physics hand-checked: an electron in a circular orbit is accelerating, so classical electromagnetism requires it to radiate continuously and spiral into the nucleus in about 10⁻⁸ s, and the frequency of that radiation would rise smoothly as the orbit shrank, giving a continuous spectrum rather than the sharp lines that are measured.

recall_prompt: Describe Rutherford's model of the atom, then give its two drawbacks with the reason for each.

steps.label: The nucleus
steps.mark_note: Charge and mass at the centre
lines: Rutherford atom model:
1. The entire positive charge and most of the
mass of the atom are concentrated at the centre
of the atom. This centre is called the nucleus.
2. The size of the nucleus is very small
compared with the size of the atom — about
10⁻¹⁵ m against 10⁻¹⁰ m.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Two things: charge and mass at the centre, and the nucleus is tiny.
steps.why: Both points come straight from the scattering experiment: the few α-particles turned right around show the charge is concentrated, and the very small fraction turned at all shows the target is tiny.
common_mistakes: Saying the positive charge is spread through the atom. That is Thomson's model.
Leaving out the size comparison. The nucleus is about 10⁻⁵ times the atom across.

recall.must_convey: That the whole positive charge and most of the mass sit in a very small nucleus at the centre.
accept: positive charge and most of the mass at the centre
the nucleus is very small compared to the atom

steps.memory_tip: All the charge, nearly all the mass, in one hundred-thousandth of the width.

steps.label: The electrons
lines: 3. The electrons revolve around the nucleus in
circular orbits, in the same way that the
planets move round the sun. The electrostatic
attraction of the nucleus supplies the
centripetal force.
4. Most of the space inside the atom is empty.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Circular orbits held by the Coulomb attraction, and the atom is mostly empty space.
steps.why: The empty space is the direct reading of the experiment: almost every α-particle went straight through the foil, which can only happen if there is very little in the way.
common_mistakes: Saying the electrons are at rest. A static electron would fall into the nucleus at once.
Leaving out what holds the electron in its orbit — the electrostatic attraction.

recall.must_convey: That electrons revolve in circular orbits held by the nucleus's attraction, and most of the atom is empty.
accept: coulomb attraction provides the centripetal force
most of the atom is empty space

steps.memory_tip: A tiny heavy centre, orbiting electrons, and empty space between.

steps.label: No stable atom
lines: Drawbacks:
1. It could not explain the stability of the
atom. An electron moving in a circular orbit is
accelerating, so by classical theory it must
radiate energy all the time. It would lose
energy, spiral inwards and reach the nucleus in
about 10⁻⁸ s. Atoms in fact last.
steps.margin_note: First drawback. Accelerating charge radiates, the orbit shrinks, the atom collapses.
steps.why: This is the flaw that Bohr's stationary-orbit postulate was written to remove: Bohr stated that an electron in an allowed orbit does not radiate.
common_mistakes: Saying the electron radiates because it moves. Uniform motion does not radiate; acceleration does.
Giving no time scale. About 10⁻⁸ s makes the failure concrete.

recall.must_convey: That the orbiting electron accelerates, radiates and spirals into the nucleus, so the model gives no stable atom.
accept: cannot explain the stability of the atom

steps.memory_tip: Circle means acceleration; acceleration means radiation; radiation means collapse.

steps.label: No line spectrum
lines: 2. It could not explain the line spectra of
atoms. As the orbit shrinks the frequency of
the emitted radiation would rise smoothly, so
the model predicts a continuous spectrum.
Atoms in fact give sharp lines at fixed
wavelengths.
steps.margin_note: Second drawback. Continuous spectrum predicted, line spectrum observed.
steps.why: Sharp lines need fixed energy levels, and Rutherford's model has none — the orbit can have any radius, so the emitted frequency can take any value. Bohr's quantum condition is what fixes this.
common_mistakes: Saying no radiation is predicted. A continuous spectrum is predicted.
Naming a drawback without the reason. Both marks are for the reason.

recall.must_convey: That the model predicts a continuous spectrum while atoms give sharp line spectra.
reject: the electron spirals into the nucleus

steps.memory_tip: Any radius means any frequency — a band, not lines.

insider_note: The model is two marks and the drawbacks two — write the reason under each drawback, because the bare statement earns half of it.
